Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Kansas statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Kansas property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Taxpayer may appeal to the county appraiser within 30 days of the mailing date of the notice of value. (Equalization Appeal Process for Real Property (K.S.A. 79-1448); source)
  • Informal hearings must be held by May 15 and results mailed by May 20. (Equalization Appeal Process for Real Property (K.S.A. 79-1496); source)
  • After the supplemental notice of final value, the taxpayer may appeal to BOTA within 30 days of its mailing date. (Equalization Appeal Process for Real Property (K.S.A. 79-1496); source)
  • Petition for reconsideration of a BOTA decision must be filed with BOTA within 15 days; judicial review in district court within 30 days. (Equalization Appeal Process for Real Property (K.S.A. 74-2426, 77-601 et seq.); source)
  • Residential property is assessed at 11.5% of appraised value. (Slide 6: Kansas Property Classification System; source)
  • A taxpayer must choose one appeal path for the same tax year: appeal at valuation notice (equalization) or pay under protest (K.S.A. 79-2005), not both. (Slide 14: Kansas Provides Appeal Rights; source)
  • BOTA has a Small Claims Division for most residential and smaller-value commercial properties. (Slide 14: Kansas Provides Appeal Rights; source)
  • Redemption period for real estate bid off by the county is 2 years (1 year for abandoned structures; 3 years for homesteads and other real estate). (K.S.A. 79-2401a; source)
  • Redeeming party pays the sale amount plus accrued interest, delinquent taxes and special assessments, and costs of sale and redemption. (K.S.A. 79-2401a(a); source)

How to sell a Kansas house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the title company needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in Kansas.

What a cash sale of a Kansas house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Kansas.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Kansas disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Kansas

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Kansas change, so confirm details with the official office or a Kansas attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Kansas

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

  • The constitutional homestead is not exempt from sale for taxes or for obligations contracted to purchase the premises or erect improvements. (Kansas Constitution Art. 15, s. 9; source)
  • Kansas offers a homestead property tax refund (Form K-40H) rather than a property tax exemption; 2025 maximum refund is $700. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • 2025 K-40H eligibility: household income of $43,389 or less and born before Jan 1, 1970, or blind/disabled, or with a qualifying dependent child. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • K-40PT (age 65+, household income $25,380 or less) refunds property tax; K-40SVR income limit is $58,041. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • 2025 claims are filed after Dec 31, 2025 and no later than April 15, 2026. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • First $75,000 of appraised value of residential property is exempt from the statewide school finance mill levy (as of 2024). (Kansas Property Tax Exemptions (KDOR); source)

content:
Kansas Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Kansas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero closing costs

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Kansas statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Kansas evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord may terminate for unpaid rent after written notice and 3 days (three consecutive 24-hour periods); mailing adds 2 days. (K.S.A. 58-2564(b); source)
  • For material noncompliance, written notice terminates the agreement not less than 30 days after receipt if not remedied in 14 days. (K.S.A. 58-2564(a); source)
  • Landlord files a petition; hearing is set within 3 to 14 days of filing. (Housing - Kansas Self-Help; source)
  • If the tenant contests, a bench trial is set within 14 days of the hearing date. (Housing - Kansas Self-Help; source)
  • A granted eviction produces a writ of restitution executed within 14 days; the court process can take up to 42 days. (Housing - Kansas Self-Help; source)
  • A landlord who conveys premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance. (K.S.A. 58-2554(a); source)
  • The seller landlord remains liable for any security deposit the tenant is entitled to. (K.S.A. 58-2554(a); source)
